Character Diaries. They give a little insight in the current life of NPC's.
Local legends. Every old town, city and even village has their own stories or heroes, horrors or village idi*ts from the past.
Old news papers / flyers
History books, for world lore
Cook books.

Take men
Hit men on head
Cook men

Hit man hard
Hit man more
Put man in fire
Eat man

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
Guess I'm one of the outliers on this, too.  But, it's a conditional outlier.
The Lore I enjoy reading is generally what most devs put in as "exposition dumps" in their games.  The main reason for this is "in case I have a question".
Generally speaking, if a dev just shows me that Elves are descriminated against in the game, I will accept the premise and move on.  But, sometimes, I want to know why they are descriminated against.  Lore is good for telling me that.
The Elder Scrolls usually has "books of Lore" in it, but they're so full of nonsense, fluff, obfuscation, and are so vague that you can't take them seriously, much less enjoy reading them.  But, the books I did like reading in the Elder Scrolls games were ones that told stories (Yes, I loved reading The Lusty Argonian Maid because it was like reading a child's attempt to write a dirty story while also being able to tell their parents it wasn't a dirty a story if they got caught.  I also loved reading the story about the guy who wanted to learn Water Breathing to rob a sunken ship).  Meanwhile, when I played Mass Effect 1, I spent a ton of time in the Lore sections of the game because I had a lot of questions and it turned out the devs had REALLY fleshed out their world and REALLY did a lot of research on what that universe would look like.
I like Lore to exist in most games, but I like it to ONLY answer questions I might have.  I like it to do the job of "exposition dump" that devs frequently toss into their cutscenes.
In this way, it's optional (because sometimes I just hate reading Lore, especially if it's boring or not well thought out and contradicts itself) as well as potentially useful if I care about the story of the world it is in.
I mean, Mass Effect 1 had Lore for each of their weapon attachments and how they worked, and it was really great Lore that made a lot of sense.  That game is probably the most "in depth" I've ever seen video game Lore go, and it went way harder than it had to, which is probably why I loved that game so much, and hated the sequels that destroyed most of that Lore.
What game, other than Mass Effect 1 would spend time explaining to you how the Mass Effect fields worked (as shielding) and THEN tell you that the reason you don't "repel chairs" when you go to sit down is because you weaken the field in those locations automatically when you go to sit so your butt can actually make contact with the chair.  Who thinks about that except someone who REALLY cares about their world?
Anyway, I love Lore like that.  Stuff that exists because I go to try to poke a hole in the logic, and so I go to read about it or whatever, and oh, no, dev thought of that hole in logic and here's the explanation.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I'm probably one of the few people who really doesn't care about the Lore of the FromSoft games.  I care primarily about the "primary story/motivation" and that's about it.  The rest of it teeters too far into "rampant speculation", which means you also have to guess whether or not something was "intentional" by the devs or not.  Which, I'm just not a fan of that.  When the Lore of your world relies heavily on trying to figure out if the devs put something in the game with intent to add to lore, or it's just there because "it's easier game design and we had to meet a deadline", then it sort of loses meaning for me.
Heck, just the weird speculation about the guy in Dark Souls 1 who pets an invisible cat is wild.  Did the devs intentionally mean to imply the guy is insane?  Or... is it an oversight and they couldn't get a cat to sit in the basket?
This says nothing of "only the undead respawn", yet every monster in the games except bosses respawn.  Does that mean these Drakes I killed are Undead, too?  What about the sewer monsters?  The Trees?  The lizard frog things?  How come even the undead bosses don't respawn?
Games that invite that kind of "speculation", really don't do themselves any favors in the story department.  But, they do make pretty fantastic content for YouTubers, so I guess that sort of thing exists to get free advertising from YouTubers, who then do it to make ad revenue money.
But, I'm just not up for that kind of storytelling.  Even in games that aren't FromSoft games.  The minute I have to go to a secondary source to "know what's going on" or "to hear speculation on what's going on", that's when I know the story is only vague to get free advertising from YouTubers.
Or, at least, that's my assumption.  My other assumptions would just be "badly translated", "badly written", or "trying to be too artsy fartsy and staring at your own belly button while inviting the audience to do the same".
None of these things really appeal to me.
It's easier for me to just think, "story doesn't matter" in such games and ignore it entirely.  Gives me a more positive impression of the media that way.

Some great comments above.
I particularly resonate most with "lore should never replace storytelling".
Lore implies that the developers have really thought about creating a world and that beyond the story in the game, other stuff happens/happened/will happen. I'd argue that lore greatly gains in value if there is much more than a single game in the series/universe.
With everything we design and make, there will be those who like our style or it matches their itch; and those who critique because it's not interesting to them, for various valid reasons.
A friend of mine, HATES flashbacks. It kind of links into the topic of lore because he'd rather have chronological story-telling and reveals rather than showing us as a side-note what the motives or plot catalysts were.
Star Wars, George Lucas, got lucky, but it worked. He created a universe and it actually worked. It could have flopped. The line was thin between acceptance and discarded, in early release and marketing. You just have to commit, and take a risk. Bit make it interesting, hopefully in a unique way to you that shows off why you as a game developer are who you are.

I like it one way, you like it another way, and pretty much everyone else from the forum likes it yet another way. Please don't let that encourage you to create the game YOU would like to play.
It is way more important that if you make a library, that everything works as intended. Those who don't like it, can skip it, and those who love it, will return time after time.
When it comes to taste (as in who likes what) you can check which opinions are more popular, but in the end this shouldn't bend your own ways just to meet their expectations. Specially since the people who give their opinion now and the people who will play your game later, are most likely not the same people. Could be that most people here say "no lore books for me", while your players shout "love them, keep them coming". Or the other way around.
And to top that, if you do what you want to do, and you do it well, it will bend people with a negative initial opinion into a positive opinion. While doing it badly will turn fans into haters. So, do what YOU prefer, and make it look fantastic. Once it is done, people will recognize quality.

The history of the world is part of the storyline - it's the story of the setting. I'd much rather find out the history of a place by doing something that has me figure it out diagetically rather than dumping exposition on me with a book.
You can do the same job as a lore library with environmental design and storytelling, NPC dialogue, character design, quest design, and even the art direction and geomorphology of your world - it's just
harder to do
than having an optional library where you can read about "THE GREAT WAR OF ABSTIRINTHIA" or whatever. Like sure, you can infodump a book on the player, but what's more interesting? Finding out about the world organically through your interactions with it, or reading a wall of text about a bunch of places and events you don't necessarily have any investment in.
Hell, even die hard fans who 'can't get enough of your main storyline' should probably be experts in your game's storyline and setting by the time they finish the game. Supplementary material can actively undermine this enjoyment if your world's Lore is - for example - worse than what they figured out in their heads.
A little aside about Dark Souls (which I'll talk about again later in this post) and the dangers of Lore delivered after the fact:
I know that Dark Souls 3's DLC which combined the games' settings into a cohesive whole was way less interesting/satisfying to me (and a lot of other players) than the mindmap the fanbase had come to post DaS1 and DaS2 - even if it is very, very cool in and of itself.
Making things explicit weakened the core game, because it wasn't as interesting as players had previously thought. A lot of people thought it was cool, and I can certainly agree that it
is cool
, but it being so explicit and definite was antithetical to the way the story had been told up until that point, and for a lot of players this made the games actively worse.
EDIT
: examples of other instances of Lore and and needless explanation retroactively weakening their constituent products:
Star Wars - midichlorians and a lot of over explanation undermines what is basically a morality play where a robot throws a wizard down a well
Zelda - the official timeline clarification and Hyrule Historia are infinitely less interesting than previous fan theories. Ambiguity led to a more effective product.
Star Trek - food replicators are reconstituted faeces! This means Picard was in fact drinking piss, Earl Grey, hot! We don't understand our own internal workings and this revisionism is now 'lore accurate'!
If you separate Lore and storyline, you're missing a trick. Your setting and your story should be intertwined - and I think this is my core objection to "standalone Lore" as a separate element of an RPG's content design. Teach me the setting and history by having me interact with the world and through the characters who dwell within it.
Like I said: Show, don't tell.

This bit is gonna be a little long, so apologies in advance for my lack of brevity here:
I
love
the concept of Lore, especially when executed well. I'm a big Dark Souls guy and I could tell you the history of that world from theories strung together from item descriptions and bizarre little single-line NPCs. I know who people are and where they're from from their armour designs, and from their place in the world - and I've spent dozens of hours piecing this stuff together for myself.
For example, Astora is the originator of the legend of the "Chosen Undead" and we know that because Astora's gear is more faith heavy than other pieces, and a knight of Astora is at the Undead Asylum (driving himself mad to try to become the person of prophecy). That legend then permeates the whole game - and it's entirely optional to learn about, which makes you feel smarter for figuring it out.
What the game
does not do
is give me a book titled "
The History of Astora
" or "
The Undead Curse
". The Lore element of the game is woven into the storytelling in a much more organic way, and creates a (largely) unique experience. One in which the player is in a tightly designed world with an ecology based around several nations and ancient prophecy, but interacts with the Lore through environment design, game design, and is drip-fed item descriptions which are intrinsically tied to exploration, and the player's progression.
Removing that experience or just straight up telling the player would make the storytelling of the setting worse, and the "Lore" less rewarding to figure out. It'd also undermine the central theming of the game.
As I said in my first post in the thread - Lore Books are (in my opinion) a crutch for poor storytelling. Not because I don't understand the distinction people draw, or necessarily conflate the two concepts, but because if you design one without understanding how you explore the other, you're missing a trick.
Anyway, I appreciate that this was probably too long of a post, but I wanted to clarify because
I love complex lore
and I love games/books/whatever that have it.
I just think that it's weak sauce to be like 'and here is a library containing the history of the world' when you could put in more effort to your game's narrative and explore it organically. It's a missed opportunity to do something more interesting, higher effort, or just plain more effective with your setting's design and conveyance.
The only thing having a lore library does, near as I can see, is let people skip the part where they have to think: "how do I fold this into the player's experience." They can just dump it in one place and say: "Look, my setting's really complicated! It has 14986149 years of charted history and the names of rivers and there's a magic crystal that controls morality!"
It's a way to make your game look like it has a better story/setting than it does.
Like I said: A crutch.

So, this here is a problem I think some people can have. Hell, this is what ultimately screwed up Hello Neighbor.
Much as I don't mind finding books with lore tidbits in them, this isn't something a dev should just aim to have while creating. You start to run the risk of focusing more on lore and less on the events actually happening in your world in the present.
To put this concisely: Don't make the game about the lore, make the game.
As for conveying your lore to players, while books are a method I'm okay with, they should not be the only method used. Look at Kingdom Hearts. Everything we know of the lore has all pretty much been mentioned verbally, implied by what we're shown or given to us through text reports. In the case of the text reports, they're journal entries that give us a character's account of things they themselves experienced.
Consider the Keyblade. Nothing about that weapon is told to us through a book in the game. In fact, there's very little concrete info given at all. What we are given are events in the game and context clues that tell us interesting things. For instance, the game does a wonderful job in setting up the reveal that Riku was meant to receive the Keyblade, not Sora.
Before we're ever told this, we see Riku actually hold the Keyblade during a scene in Traverse Town, having snatched it from Sora without the other even realizing. It's framed as a minor comedic exchange, but it's given importance when you remember that the game showed another character, Leon, take hold of the Keyblade back at the beginning of the game. In Leon's case, the Keyblade straight up vanished from his hand and reappeared in Sora's hand.
So, what does any of that have to do with lore? A lot, actually. By the time you complete the story within Hollow Bastion, you are able to infer that the Keyblade has some level of sentience based on the way it refused to be held by Leon, as well as the fact that despite it meaning to go to Riku, Sora is ultimately able to command it fully and completely, willing it right out of Riku's hand. It shifted allegiance over to Sora after Sora proved his worth.
Note that this is just in the first game.

I mean no offense when I say this, but "heart and soul" is not a thing that moves the needle, skill is. Passion is excellent, but if you can't execute, or you're making something no-one wants, that's a good thing to know
as early into production as possible
so that you can course correct.
Figuring out what your audience wants and actually executing on it is
absolutely vital
. It's why starting this thread was a really good shout from OP; there's nothing better than actually finding out what people think, and discussions like this I think are really healthy - especially when people disagree.
Effort
is
a decent metric - but efficacy is more important. As I (and others) keep saying, if you're spending all that time writing Lore Books, why not do something else with that effort that will move the needle more?
Usually, it has a really, really simple answer: Writing Lore is fun, and literally anyone on the planet can do it because all it requires is your imagination and a pen.
Worldbuilding is fun. In more cases than not though, it is a distraction from getting other stuff done - and in a lot of cases ends up being a crutch for "worldbuilding" that tricks developers into complacency. After all, they don't need to make custom art, or do the legwork to make their characters believable; all the flaws in their story and plot holes can be handwaved because it's all explained in the Lore Books, after all.

I think you highly underestimate how hard it is to write 100 little stories that at first glance seem unrelated, but all together write one large story. If that is done right, than that is actually mighty impressive.
Click to expand...
I
really
don't underestimate this. Narrative design (which is what this is, not writing) is a really complex skill which requires years to master. The issue is that good narrative design and bad narrative design - and the content/featuresets that come with them look super similar to developers, so without that foundational experience you can really easily end up in a hole of your own digging.
An example, in the form of a up:
My RM game currently has like 80,000 words of flavour text in an effort to bolster interactivity, a lot of which ties into little strings laid across the world for people to find.
It's a ton of effort, and a smarter man would have realised that no-one's ever going to read it, but because of the commitment I find myself painted into a corner having to fill the world with text that very few people will ever care about.
Why did I do that? Well, reason one is that it's fun and I enjoy writing - so, self-indulgence. Reason two is that I thought it'd help underpin narrative and flesh out the setting; but so few people when testing actually engage with it that it has proved not to be a good use of time. One which slows down development, adds additional passes to every map in the game, and because inconsistency is a key marker of low quality - one I can't just back out of.
It doesn't move the needle, and while one in a hundred people might engage with some of it, it's going to prove to be a massive waste of time which will lower my overall quality. It's something I shouldn't have done, so I don't know why I'd encourage other people to pursue similar content.

If lore books are added just as an easy way to blur out content, then yes, that is lazy. But if it is done right, than this actually takes more effort than you might think.

I think it's much more damaging (and disresepectful) to look a person in the eye and say "this optional Lore Book is high value content", though. Doubly so if you're detracting from your core feature set to spend time on something "easier", or "more fun", and convincing yourself it's content that is going to help tip the balance of your project into "good game" territory.

benefit
from the ambiguity of not over-explaining themselves. Then you find their lore library and it's literally just
MYWORLD.TXT
dumped into 15 unformatted text boxes and you realise that they don't respect their audience's time, and would rather tell you their ideas about a fantasy setting than create a cohesive and compelling video game.

If you are the only person in the world who enjoys Lore Books, you shouldn't be telling devs to waste their time to make you happy, in my view - you should be encouraging them to do things that actually move the needle and contribute to what the majority of the audience for their game enjoys.

For me, it needs to be relevant to the characters in some way. If it has no effect, then what's the point? Ex: does a character act a certain way because of a law set in place by a civilization from an event that happened years ago? I don't like having to read a huge dump of lore. It's better when slowly introduced in the gameplay. It's helpful to have a character unknowing to things happening/things that have happened, because then they can ask questions, and then they can be reasonably answered. But a character shouldn't strictly exist to ask questions, that makes them seem boring and repetitive in my opinion. No lore placement should be too long, if a player finds a hidden book explaining everything about how their world was created, will they read the entire thing? More than likely, no. Especially if it's not impacting the gameplay in any way. Some players do enjoy lore placements like that, but a lot of the time it doesn't seem worth the time.
You could have your own world/universe or whatever with extremely detailed lore, and you'd want to share it, of course! it could be extremely good. But whether it's actually well written/detailed, or engaging or not, it's good to leave the player to interpret some aspects. Giving clues to certain things instead of just saying "this is exactly what happened and why". It can make the player more interested in the lore, as it's their choice whether or not they want to take in those clues and figure it out for themselves. It's always satisfying for me when I find something that's connected to each other on my own while playing a game or reading a book.
